Ch . 2
In 1798, Congress imposed a direct tax on all real estate in all 
states. The taxable value of every land parcel was determined by 
federal assessors according to what they found the land to be “worth 
in money.” The legislation did not define this phrase or require any 
particular method of valuation. Additionally, the legislation 
estabhshed, for each state, a federal board with power to divide the 
state into districts and raise or lower the taxable value of all parcels 
within any district en masse by any percentage “as shall appear to be 
just and equitable,” again with no definitions or required methods. 
Nor was there any backgroimd consensus on how to do real estate 
valuation. On the contrary, region-wide mass tax valuation of the 
kind undertaken by the federal boards was notoriously contested and 
pohticized when done by state legislatures for state property taxes. 
Nicholas R. Parrillo, A Critical Assessment of the Originalist Case 
Against Administrative Regulatory Power, 130 Yale L.J. 1288 (2021).
Originahst proponents of a categorical prohibition against rulemaking 
reconcile such statutes with their theory by claiming the prohibition has 
certain categorical exceptions. As to things like disabled soldiers’ pay, postal 
services, or disabled seamen’s health care, there is said to be an exception for 
non-coercive matters Eke benefits and government services. As to things like 
trading with Native Americans and laying embargoes, there is said to be an 
exception for foreign affairs. As to things like the “just and equitable” mass 
revision of taxable land values, there is said to be an exception for rules that 
turn upon fact-finding. E.g., Hamburger, Nondelegation Blues, supra, at 1202— 
14; Gordon, supra. Other scholars respond that the few lawmakers who 
invoked a nondelegation principle in Congress during the 1790s often did so in 
ways that didn’t recognize exceptions for non-coercive or foreign matters, 
Mortenson & Bagley, supra, at 363; Kevin Arlyck, Delegation, Administration, 
and Improvisation, 97 Notre Dame L. Rev. 243, 286-95 (2021), and that an 
exception for fact-finding expansive enough to cover decisions as sweeping, 
methodless, and contestable as the “just and equitable” revisions of tax 
valuations will have no clear boundaries, Parrillo, Nondelegation, Original 
Meaning, and Early Federal Taxation: A Dialogue with My Critics, 71 Drake 
L. Rev. 367 (2024).
Other originalist proponents of a tougher nondelegation doctrine do not 
press the claim for a categorical prohibition on rulemaking but instead adopt 
a more open-ended approach, often centered on the distinction drawn in 
Wayman between “important subjects which must be entirely regulated by the 
legislature itself’ and subjects “of less interest” for which administrators may 
“fill up the details.” E.g., Wurman, supra; Gary Lawson, Delegation and 
Original Meaning, 88 Va. L. Rev. 327, 396-403 (2002). In response, some 
scholarship has argued that early Congresses did not operate on a principle 
that “important” matters were non-delegable, as that term was used by 
contemporaries. Christine Kexel Chabot, The Lost History of Delegation at the 
Founding, 56 Ga. L. Rev. 81 (2021). It may be, however, that a nondelegation
